title: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre
wiki_lead:
The Texas Chain Saw Massacre is a 1974 American slasher film  produced, co-composed, and directed by Tobe Hooper, who co-wrote it with Kim Henkel. The film stars Marilyn Burns, Paul A. Partain, Edwin Neal, Jim Siedow, and Gunnar Hansen. The plot follows a group of friends who fall victim to a family of cannibals while on their way to visit an old homestead. The independent film was marketed as being based on true events to attract a wider audience and to act as a subtle commentary on the era's political climate. Although the character of Leatherface and minor story details were inspired by the crimes of murderer Ed Gein, its plot is largely fictional.
Hooper produced the film for less than $140,000 ($700,000 adjusted for inflation) and used a cast of relatively unknown actors drawn mainly from central Texas, where the film was shot. Due to the film's violent content, Hooper struggled to find a distributor, but it was eventually acquired by the Bryanston Distributing Company. Hooper limited the quantity of onscreen gore in hopes of securing a PG rating, but the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) rated it R. The film faced similar difficulties internationally, being banned in several countries, and numerous theaters stopped showing the film in response to complaints about its violence.
The Texas Chain Saw Massacre was released in the United States on October 11, 1974.  While the film initially received mixed reception from critics, it was highly profitable, grossing over $30 million at the domestic box office, equivalent with roughly over $205 million as of 2026, selling over 16.5 million tickets in 1974. It has since become widely regarded as one of the best and most influential horror films. It is credited with originating several elements common in the slasher genre: the use of power tools as murder weapons; the characterization of the killer as a large, hulking, masked figure; and the final girl. It led to a franchise that continued the story of Leatherface and his family through sequels, prequels, a remake, comic books, and video games. In 2024, the film was selected for preservation in the United States National Film Registry by the Library of Congress as being "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant".

Plot
In the early hours of August 18, 1973, a grave robber steals several corpses from a cemetery near the fictional town of Newt, Muerto County, Texas. The robber ties a rotting corpse and other body parts onto a monument, creating a grisly display that is discovered by a local resident as the sun rises.
Five teenagers — Sally Hardesty, Jerry, Pam, Kirk, and Sally's paraplegic brother Franklin — take a road trip through the area in a van. They stop at the cemetery to check on the grave of Sally and Franklin's grandfather, which appears undisturbed. grok_lead: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre is a 1974 American independent horror film directed by Tobe Hooper, who co-wrote the screenplay with Kim Henkel and served as co-producer and co-composer. The story depicts five friends driving through rural Texas in search of an abandoned farmhouse, only to encounter a depraved, cannibalistic family including the masked killer Leatherface, who wields a chainsaw as his primary weapon. Produced on a shoestring budget estimated at $140,000, the film achieved extraordinary commercial success by grossing approximately $30.9 million domestically, demonstrating the viability of low-cost, high-impact independent filmmaking in the horror genre. Shot in a gritty, quasi-documentary style with natural lighting and minimal special effects to heighten realism, it initially provoked outrage for its unrelenting depictions of violence and decay, leading to bans in several countries including the United Kingdom until 1999, yet this raw approach has cemented its status as a foundational slasher film that shifted horror toward visceral, human-centered terror over supernatural elements. Despite early critical pans labeling it "despicable," retrospective acclaim has elevated it to a cult classic, spawning a franchise of sequels, remakes, and prequels while influencing directors through its emphasis on psychological dread and familial dysfunction as sources of horror.
